title: Six Months Before Anyone Would Borrow: Kashf's First Loans in Lahore
dek: Roshaneh Zafar left the World Bank, studied Grameen and its neighbours, and in 1996 spent months winning the trust of Lahore's women before Kashf made its first 15 loans.

story.event: Founding Kashf and making its first microloans to women in Lahore
story.summary: After four years at the World Bank in Islamabad and ten weeks with Grameen Bank, where Muhammad Yunus urged her to work in Pakistan and offered $10,000, Roshaneh Zafar studied microfinance across South Asia and registered Kashf in Lahore in June 1996. Its five-woman team waited months before anyone would borrow, then made its first 15 loans, of about 4,000 rupees each, in November 1996. Kashf became the first financially sustainable microfinance institution in Pakistan and had more than 300,000 clients by 2009.
paragraphs: In November 1996, the five women who made up Kashf's staff in Lahore made its first 15 loans, averaging about 4,000 rupees, roughly $80, each. Roshaneh Zafar, the founder, was one of the loan officers. The first loan, she later recalled, paid for a little grocery store; others went on poultry, two goats, a vegetable stall and a catering business.

After degrees at Wharton and Yale, Zafar spent four years at the World Bank in Islamabad, where work on hygiene took her to women across Pakistan who, she said, were struggling to earn an income while "fighting all sorts of social norms." At a conference in Islamabad she had sat beside Muhammad Yunus of Bangladesh's Grameen Bank, and they kept in touch. When she left the Bank and told him she was out of work, he bought her a ticket to Bangladesh. She spent ten weeks with Grameen and wanted a job there. Yunus told her, "Pakistan needs you more than Bangladesh," and offered $10,000 to start something when she was ready.

She did not simply copy Grameen. She spent about a year studying lenders in India and Nepal, with interns from the INSEAD business school helping on a feasibility study, and registered Kashf in June 1996 with Yunus's money and small Swiss and Dutch grants. It asked for no collateral, sent staff to borrowers, and lent to groups of five women who shared responsibility for repayment. For months nobody would borrow; she later put it at about six. People assumed, she said, that there had to be a hidden agenda. What changed their minds was that the staff kept their appointments, even in rain or hail. Borrowers then went through about three months of training, which for some included learning to sign their names.

In 1999 Kashf added a consumption loan for women and in 2001 insurance, and by Zafar's account it became, in 2003, the first microfinance institution in Pakistan to be financially sustainable. By 2009 it had more than 300,000 clients, and it later opened a microfinance bank. By 2011 borrowers paid an effective interest rate of about 35 per cent; Kashf itself borrowed from banks at 14 to 16 per cent. In 2019 Zafar said it had 535,000 clients.

quote.text: He who lightly promises is sure to keep but little faith; he who is continually thinking things easy is sure to find them difficult. Therefore the sage sees difficulty even in what seems easy, and so never has any difficulties.
quote.source_title: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics, tr. James Legge, Project Gutenberg eBook #216
quote.connection: Kashf won its first borrowers not with promises but by turning up when it said it would, in any weather. Laozi ties trust to the weight of a promise and warns that whoever thinks a thing easy will find it hard; Zafar spent a year studying before she lent anything.

reflection: For about six months, nobody took a loan from Kashf. From outside that might have looked like failure. Inside, the staff were doing the only work that could change it: arriving when they had said they would, whatever the weather.

Some of your own work is like that. Trust from a colleague, a patient or your family is built from promises small enough to keep, kept many times. It rarely appears on any list of achievements, and on a tired day it is easy to undervalue. It may be worth counting it anyway.
invitation: Think of one promise you made lightly this week: a call, a reply, a small favour. Either keep it today, or tell the person honestly when you will.

cross_checks.claim: Kashf was founded in Lahore in 1996
Kashf's first loans went to 15 women in 1996
Zafar worked at the World Bank in Islamabad before meeting Yunus, who inspired and helped fund Kashf with $10,000
Zafar studied microfinance models in India and Nepal before planning Kashf
Kashf became Pakistan's first financially sustainable microfinance institution
Kashf had more than 300,000 clients by 2009 to 2011

research_notes: Founding date: PBS (2011) says Zafar started Kashf in 1995; Zafar's own account to Knowledge at Wharton says preliminary work began in 1995 and Kashf was registered in June 1996, with the first loans in November 1996; FMO and Vital Voices give 1996. The story uses June 1996 for registration and November 1996 for the first loans. Her time at Grameen: Wharton has ten weeks, Incofin 'three months' before Yunus suggested she go home; the story uses ten weeks. The $10,000: Wharton calls it a loan offered by Yunus, Incofin a cheque he never reclaimed; the story says he 'offered $10,000' without calling it either. The 'about six months' before anyone borrowed is Zafar's recollection and sits loosely with June registration and November first loans (preliminary work began in 1995), so the story attributes it to her. Client numbers vary by date and measure: over 301,000 in 2009 (Vital Voices), about 300,000 active clients in 2011 (Wharton, PBS), 340,000 in 2017 (FMO), 535,000 in 2019 (Incofin); Wharton's summary also mentions 1 million women reached in total, a cumulative figure not used. The 2003 sustainability milestone rests on Zafar's account (Wharton) and Vital Voices' profile. The interest-rate comparison is from PBS's report and is stated without comment. The Vital Voices page names her World Bank department as Water and Sanitation; Wharton describes the work as social sector development; the story says only that work on hygiene took her to women across Pakistan. Zafar's first-person essay in Stanford Social Innovation Review (2011) could not be extracted from its PDF and is not cited. The Laozi passage closes chapter 63, which begins with doing great things while they are small.
